impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating the jury verdict that Lilly willfully infringed Teva's headache patents covering anti-CGRP antibody treatments. This case involves blockbuster migraine drugs and has major implications for the scope of written description and enablement requirements for antibody patents in the pharmaceutical industry.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to obtain and enforce broad antibody claims, particularly in the lucrative migraine/headache therapeutic space, by clarifying that genus claims covering humanized antibodies can satisfy § 112 requirements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar companies face greater risk of infringement liability for antibody-based therapeutics, potentially delaying market entry and increasing costs.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the '953 patent could claim priority from a provisional application where the issued patent changed a substituent definition from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl,' allegedly correcting an obvious typographical error, and whether Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir anticipated the claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment that Enanta's patent covering coronavirus replication inhibitors was invalid as anticipated. The court held that the change from C2 to C1 in the alkyl group definition was not an obvious typographical error, so the patent could not claim priority from its provisional application, and Pfizer's intervening disclosure of nirmatrelvir (the active ingredient in Paxlovid) anticipated the claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Protects Pfizer's ability to market Paxlovid without patent liability to Enanta, reinforcing the importance of careful provisional application drafting and the high bar for correcting alleged typographical errors in priority documents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent applicants face significant risk that even minor drafting errors in provisional applications cannot be corrected in non-provisional filings, potentially losing priority dates and exposing claims to intervening prior art.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in the weight-to-weight ratio limitation of the '282 patent, and whether the court erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal of a preliminary injunction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction barring Hetero from launching a generic competitor to Nuedexta but vacated the district court's waiver of the bond requirement pending appeal. The ruling preserves Otsuka's market exclusivity for its neurological disorder drug through patent expiration while requiring a bond to protect the generic manufacturer.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from affirmation that preliminary injunctions can block generic entry where patent infringement is likely, preserving market exclusivity during litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face delayed market entry and lost revenue, though the vacatur of the bond waiver provides some financial protection if the injunction is later reversed.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether the court properly struck certain damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent against Intel, finding error in at least one of the district court's grounds for summary judgment. The case involves significant damages claims in the semiconductor industry and addresses the extraterritorial reach of U.S. patent law for processor technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of semiconductor and processor technology patents benefit from a broader interpretation of territorial reach and doctrine of equivalents theories.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies like Intel face renewed infringement liability and potential large damages awards in cases involving widely deployed processor architectures.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting two invalidity grounds that were not included in its IPR petition but which it reasonably could have raised.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and inadequate accounting for hindsight bias in estopping the other. The decision clarifies the evidentiary standard for determining whether a skilled searcher conducting a diligent search reasonably could have discovered prior art references.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from a more rigorous standard for IPR estoppel, preserving their ability to assert invalidity defenses in district court litigation even after filing IPR petitions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face weakened estoppel protections, meaning defendants may have greater latitude to raise invalidity arguments in district court that were not included in their IPR petitions.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Insulet's trade secret misappropriation claim under the Defend Trade Secrets Act was time-barred where the alleged misappropriation of insulin patch pump technology occurred in 2018 and suit was filed in 2023.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict and damages award in Insulet's favor, holding that the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations had expired before Insulet brought suit. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation of its Omnipod insulin pump trade secrets by former employees who joined EOFlow well before the limitations period.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's statute of limitations, providing a definitive cutoff for liability exposure.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to discover misappropriation, or risk losing the ability to pursue DTSA claims even where misappropriation is proven.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award in a dispute over automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of the jury's breach of contract award, reinstating the original jury verdict. The decision addresses the proper framework for measuring damages in trade secret misappropriation cases under both the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret plaintiffs benefit from expanded admissibility of damages models and reinstatement of jury awards, potentially increasing recoveries in software misappropriation cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal replacements for licensed software face greater exposure to trade secret damages claims and must ensure clean-room development processes.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that each of the four asserted trade secrets was a protectable trade secret under California law, and whether the jury's finding of inventorship supported patent invalidity.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the trade secret misappropriation verdict, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets regarding cosmetic penile implants were protectable under California law because the underlying ideas were generally known. The court also reversed the patent invalidity finding, reasoning that ideas found to be generally known cannot constitute an inventive contribution for inventorship purposes. The counterfeiting claim was affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from heightened scrutiny of trade secret protectability, requiring plaintiffs to demonstrate that claimed secrets are not generally known in the field.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret plaintiffs face a higher burden to establish that asserted secrets contain non-public, protectable information, even after obtaining favorable jury verdicts.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue third parties for patent infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring an infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the right to independently bring infringement suits possesses sufficient exclusionary rights to satisfy Article III standing. The ruling clarifies standing requirements for patent owners who enter complex licensing arrangements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who license commercialization rights can preserve standing to enforce their patents by retaining litigation rights in their agreements, providing flexibility in licensing structures.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a procedural defense that could have blocked suits by patent owners who have licensed most of their patent rights to exclusive licensees.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for some claims while affirming eligibility for others, in a case involving wireless communication technology used in consumer electronics. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, preserving an $11.5 million-plus judgment on the affirmed claims. The split decision provides important guidance on § 101 eligibility for communication technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in telecommunications and digital standards benefit from affirmation that certain implementation-specific communication system claims satisfy § 101 eligibility.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers face continued infringement exposure for products incorporating standardized communication protocols, and the vacatur creates uncertainty regarding eligibility of some patent claims.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices on farming equipment are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in finding the case was not exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional for purposes of attorneys' fees. The decision continues the trend of invalidating agricultural technology patents under Alice/Mayo while signaling that meritless patent assertions may warrant fee-shifting.
impacts.positiveImplications: Agricultural technology companies accused of infringement benefit from continued strict application of § 101 to data collection and processing patents, and the remand on exceptionality opens the door to fee awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: AgTech patent holders face heightened risk that farming data automation patents will be invalidated as abstract ideas, and potential liability for attorneys' fees if assertions are found exceptional.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the on-sale bar of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that prior art sales expressly disclose the functionality of the sold device, and whether Rule 30(b)(6) deposition testimony may be considered at summary judgment regardless of the witness's personal knowledge.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that sales of a prior art device (Hypertech Power Programmer III) more than one year before the patent's priority date invalidated claims directed to engine controller reprogramming. The court confirmed that Rule 30(b)(6) testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the corporate representative lacks personal knowledge of the testified facts.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants challenging patent validity benefit from expanded use of corporate representative testimony at summary judgment and confirmation that commercial sales of a device trigger the on-sale bar regardless of whether functionality was publicly disclosed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face broader invalidity challenges based on historical product sales, with corporate testimony admissible even from representatives who were not present during the relevant time period.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination regarding sensor-based logistics patent claims, and whether a non-party to district court litigation can file IPR petitions on behalf of or in coordination with the defendant in that litigation to circumvent the one-year time bar of 35 U.S.C. § 315(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination regarding FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. The case involves Qualcomm filing IPR petitions on the same day as Roambee's filing deadline challenging patents asserted against Roambee, raising significant questions about potential abuse of the IPR system through coordinated filings by non-parties.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer scrutiny of coordinated IPR filings by non-parties that may be acting as proxies to circumvent the one-year time bar, protecting the integrity of IPR proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on third-party IPR filings to challenge patents face increased risk that such petitions will be scrutinized or denied if coordination with time-barred parties is suspected.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in its jury instructions and verdict form regarding § 101 patent eligibility, and whether a single infringement verdict question covering multiple patents without identifying which patent(s) were infringed requires a new trial.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments against ecobee and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form's use of a single infringement question covering all asserted patents was prejudicial error. The court also remanded for further proceedings on § 101 eligibility of the '495 patent while affirming eligibility of the '887 and '371 patents directed to wireless building automation systems.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that verdict forms must separately identify which patents are infringed, preventing conflated verdicts that obscure the basis for liability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders risk reversal of favorable jury verdicts where verdict forms do not require patent-by-patent findings, increasing the procedural complexity and cost of multi-patent litigation.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim terms reciting 'executable program code configured to' perform specified functions should be construed as means-plus-function terms under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), in light of intervening precedent in Dyfan, LLC v. Target Corp.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling regarding multimedia navigation patents and remanded for reconsideration under the intervening Dyfan precedent on means-plus-function analysis. The court affirmed the jury's invalidity finding for anticipation on the '638 patent. The decision signals that 'executable program code configured to' language may not automatically trigger § 112(f) treatment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders benefit from the possibility that 'executable program code configured to' claim language may avoid means-plus-function treatment, potentially broadening claim scope and surviving indefiniteness challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies accused of infringement face uncertainty regarding the scope of software method claims pending the evolving standard for means-plus-function analysis.
